claims.text: Controlled annealing can alter or enhance chemical short-range order in CrCoNi-type medium/high-entropy alloys.
Increasing chemical short-range order increases hardness in high-entropy alloys.
Increasing chemical short-range order increases alloy strength.
The strength increase caused by chemical short-range order results from higher energy barriers to dislocation motion.
A homogenized equimolar CrCoNi alloy can be prepared as a single-phase initial material.
High-temperature homogenization produces a CrCoNi-type baseline with minimal chemical short-range order.
Varying annealing temperature and duration can produce different levels or forms of chemical short-range order without changing overall alloy composition.
Annealing in an oxygen-free inert atmosphere prevents secondary-phase formation.
Local chemical order can occur within nanoclusters and can be characterized using electron nanodiffraction, neutron scattering, atom-probe tomography, or related diffraction methods.
Greater chemical short-range order creates a more rugged atomic energy landscape.
Chemical short-range order affects dislocation-slip behavior and deformation microstructure.
Chemical short-range order elevates barriers for dislocation nucleation.
Chemical short-range order can increase stacking-fault energy and promote diffuse antiphase-boundary development, thereby affecting dislocation glide and plastic-strain localization.
Samples with more induced chemical short-range order will have significantly greater yield strength than a homogenized baseline.
The extent of chemical short-range order will correlate positively and systematically with hardness and strength enhancement.
The proposed behavior is limited to single-phase, equimolar high-entropy alloys and may not apply to multiphase or compositionally segregated alloys.
Grain size, grain orientation, and related microstructural factors can also influence measured mechanical behavior.
